issues.legal_issue: Interest paid for delayed payment of compensation after compulsory acquisition is a taxable revenue receipt rather than part of capital compensation.
material_facts: The acquired land vested in the Government when possession was taken, and the owner thereafter had no title to or right to possess the land.
The award separately identified compensation for the land and interest payable from the taking of possession until payment or deposit of the compensation.
The interest was included in the recipient’s income for tax purposes, and the dispute concerned whether it was capital or revenue in nature.
issues.conclusion: The interest was compensation for the delayed payment and use of the money representing the land compensation, not compensation for the acquisition or loss of possession; it was a revenue receipt liable to tax.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 34, 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, interest is payable on the awarded compensation from possession until payment or deposit, while the land vests in the Government upon possession. Sections 15, 23 and 24 distinguish compensation for the land from interest payable after compensation is ascertained. Under sections 3 and 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the interest is taxable as a revenue receipt. The Court approved Westminster Bank Ltd. v. Riches, Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras v. C.T. B.M.N. Narayanan Chettiar, and Commissioner of Income-tax, Bihar and Orissa v. Maharajadhiraj Sir Kameshwar Singh; it overruled Behari Lal Bhargava v. Commissioner of Income-tax and P.V. Kurien v. Commissioner of Income-tax. It distinguished Inglewood Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd. v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission and Revenue Divisional Officer, Trichinopoly v. Venkatarama Ayyar because title had not passed upon possession in those cases.

predicates.legally_required_interest_for_delayed_co: The recipient was paid interest required by law because compensation was not paid or deposited when possession was taken.

issues.definition: When a tax dispute concerns legally required interest on delayed land compensation, the compensation and interest are distinct, and the recipient is divested of the land upon possession, the interest is treated as a taxable revenue receipt.

issues.legal_issue: The timing of taking possession relative to the compensation award does not alter the revenue character of statutory interest on delayed compensation.
material_facts: The Court considered the contention that interest should be treated as capital if possession was taken before the award, unlike where possession followed the award.
Under the acquisition scheme considered by the Court, title vested in the Government when possession was taken, whether possession occurred before or after the award.
The interest was payable from the taking of possession until the compensation was paid or deposited.
issues.conclusion: There is no difference in the legal character of the interest depending on whether possession is taken before or after the award; in either case it is interest for delayed payment of compensation and is a revenue receipt.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, provides for interest on compensation from the taking of possession until payment or deposit. Under sections 16 and 17, title vests in the Government upon possession, whether possession is taken after an award or, in an urgent case, before one. Because the owner has no right to retain possession after that vesting, the interest is not compensation for loss of possession. The Court distinguished Inglewood Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd. v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission and Revenue Divisional Officer, Trichinopoly v. Venkatarama Ayyar, in which title did not pass upon possession.
